title: Influence-Disentangled Federated Training
one_liner: When someone asks to delete their data from a federated model, a new method lets you do it instantly and correctly without starting over.
lead: Federated learning splits the training work across many devices (phones, hospitals, banks) so the data never leaves the source. But when someone requests deletion, their influence on the model is tangled throughout all previous rounds of training. This paper proposes a way to untangle that influence during training itself, so deletion becomes just subtraction, not retraining from scratch.

paras: Federated learning means each person's device trains on their own data, then sends a small update to a central model instead of sending raw data. The central server mixes these updates together, over many rounds. This is private by design.

But privacy law says people can request deletion: remove my data, forget me. Ideally that means the model acts as if that person was never there. The naive way: throw away the whole model and retrain without that person. For thousands of rounds of training and thousands of devices, this is impossibly slow.

The problem: after round 1, device A sends a small change to the model. Round 2, that change gets mixed with device B's change. By round 100, device A's influence is smeared everywhere — baked into millions of weights (the numbers the model actually uses to make predictions) through chains of mixing. You cannot just subtract device A's original update; the damage is done.

callout.html: This paper untangles each device's influence during training so deletion is subtraction, not a full retrain.

steps.text: Each round, split the updates into a shared part (what all devices move toward) and a per-device residual (only this device's unique change).
Use a math trick (shrinkage) to dial down the components that mix across devices; keep the cleanly separable parts.
Over all rounds, accumulate a record of each device's removable influence (the parts that can be cleanly undone).
When device A asks for deletion, subtract its entire accumulated trace from the model in one step.
Run a short retraining on the remaining devices to smooth out any small inconsistencies and restore model quality.

object.h2: The thing that changes: per-device influence traces
paras: The paper does not move weights or change training rules. Instead, it changes what is recorded. During standard federated training, each round's updates are decomposed into a shared direction (all devices nudge the model the same way) and a per-device residual (unique to one device). The residual is what matters for deletion: it is the bridge between a device's changes and the final model.

hidden.name: removable influence per device
paras: After many rounds of federated training, a device's influence is baked into the model in two ways: (1) through shared directions that all devices moved toward together, and (2) through unique residual traces that only this device made. The hidden quantity is the residual trace — the part of the model that would disappear if you removed all of that device's updates.

The paper estimates this by decomposing each update as a shared component (the average direction across all participating devices) plus a leftover (the device-specific residual). By tracking which weight changes are entangled (tied to many devices) versus separable (only this device), the algorithm learns how much of each device's influence can be cleanly removed without touching shared learning.

heat.caption: Darker means more weight; highlighted cells show cleanly removable traces; unlit shows shared learning or entangled past.

reads.html: Each device leaves fingerprints on the model. IDFT sorts those fingerprints into ones we can erase (residuals) and ones we have to leave alone (shared learning). When device A asks for deletion, we erase only its fingerprints.

The paper decomposes each round's update into a shared average and a per-device residual; applies entanglement-aware shrinkage to suppress non-removable components; tracks the removable residuals across rounds; uses them to compute the deletion update in one step.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: decomposition plus repair
paras: The core idea rests on a simple truth: if you keep a record of each device's separate contribution (not mixed in yet), you can undo it instantly. But after mixing for 100 rounds, that record is lost. IDFT recovers it by doing a lightweight decomposition every round, storing the separable parts, and throwing away the tangled parts.

Here is the mechanism. Each round, the algorithm splits the incoming updates into (1) the average of all updates (what all devices agree on, the shared learning) and (2) each device's departure from that average (the residual, only this device's unique signal). The residual is the part we can remove. But residuals from early rounds get mixed into later rounds, so the algorithm uses a shrinkage step: it dampens the components that are most entangled and keeps only the residuals that stay device-specific throughout training. Over time, this builds a clean record of each device's truly removable influence.

When deletion arrives, subtracting the residual trace undoes the device's push on the model in one shot. But because training entangled that device with others, a small inconsistency remains. A short retraining (on the remaining devices only) smooths out that inconsistency, repairing model quality to match what retraining from scratch would give.

stages.s: Split into shared average and per-device residual
On deletion: subtract trace, short repair
Model as if device was never there

math.words: the model after deletion is the current model minus the accumulated removable influence trace for that device, followed by a short retraining step on the remaining data.
symbols: the full trained model before deletion
the model after device i is removed and repaired
device i's residual update at round t (its unique signal only)
a factor (0 to 1) that suppresses entangled components; closer to 1 means we trust the residual

the small change from retraining on remaining devices only

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Device A's trace over 3 rounds: residual_round1 = 0.02, residual_round2 = 0.015 (shrinkage=0.8), residual_round3 = 0.01 (shrinkage=0.6).

Delete: theta_new = theta_current - 0.038 (the accumulated influence). Then retrain briefly on devices B, C, D to fix inconsistencies. Result: model acts like device A was never there, with quality nearly matching full retrain.

math.note: The shrinkage factor tunes how much we trust each residual; smaller shrinkage means more entanglement, so we remove less. The sum across rounds rebuilds the full influence path.

bars.h2: Retrain gap: how close deletion comes to full retraining

charts.title: Naive deletion (subtraction only)
charts.note: Subtracting round-1 updates alone leaves tangled influence; model accuracy drops sharply and does not match retrain.

charts.title: IDFT (this paper)
charts.note: IDFT tracks removable influence and repairs after deletion; model quality nearly matches full retraining but with far less compute.

items.b: Device that trained for many rounds.
items.html: If a device participated in hundreds of rounds, its influence is deeply layered; entanglement is higher, shrinkage is lower, and the residual trace is smaller. Deletion leaves more remnants and requires longer repair.

items.b: High heterogeneity (devices far apart in data).
items.html: If device A's data is very different from device B's, the shared average is less representative of any single device; residuals are larger; entanglement is harder to disentangle. The repair step takes longer.

items.b: Deletion of a large coalition of devices.
items.html: Deleting many devices at once can leave more entanglement than deleting one. The repair becomes more expensive because the model has to relearn more lost shared knowledge.

IDFT succeeds when repair is brief (a few retraining rounds on remaining data) and gap to full retrain is small. The paper shows this holds on standard benchmarks (CIFAR-10, Shakespeare, Emnist) at typical scales (100-1000 rounds, 10-100 devices).

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A demo should run federated training on a small dataset (CIFAR-10 with 20 devices, each holding 250 images) for 50 rounds. Then pick one device and delete it using IDFT: compute the residual trace, subtract it, run a 5-round repair. Compare the final model accuracy to (1) naive deletion (accuracy drops) and (2) full retrain (accuracy matches). Also measure communication cost (IDFT uses one subtraction per device; retrain needs 50 fresh rounds). Show that IDFT deletion uses 100x less communication than retrain while matching retrain's accuracy loss.
demo.metric_eq: retrain_gap = accuracy_after_IDFT_delete - accuracy_after_full_retrain; communication_ratio = rounds_in_IDFT / rounds_in_full_retrain
demo.closing: The demo must make it obvious that deletion can be instant (one subtraction) and nearly perfect (gap < 2% to retrain) without retraining the entire model from scratch.
